idiom_name: namespace per module + header/implementation pair, internals in an unnamed namespace
implementation_notes: A C++ module is a namespace (namespace acme::billing) declared in a header and implemented in one or more .cpp files; every name declared in the header is visible to all includers, because C++ has no package-private level between private and public. Implementation-only names therefore go into an unnamed namespace in the .cpp file, which gives them internal linkage (guaranteed since C++11), and the build target is the physical unit of the module. Choose C++20 named modules where the toolchain supports them: they make the interface a real boundary and remove the textual include model.
pitfalls: A namespace is a naming device, not an encapsulation boundary: every declaration in the header is reachable by includers, so 'namespace-private' does not exist - keep internal declarations out of headers.
A using-directive at global scope in a header (using namespace ...) leaks unrelated names into every client's lookup and recreates the coupling the module was meant to remove.
Because headers are textual, a cycle between two modules compiles silently; only a build-graph or module-level check detects it.

variants.name: C++20 named modules (export module / import)
variants.implementation_notes: A module unit (export module billing;) replaces the header/implementation pair: only exported declarations are visible to importers, non-exported names and macros cannot leak into them, and a private module fragment (module : private;) hides implementation even from the module's other units. Modules are orthogonal to namespaces and are normally combined with them. The price is a whole-build contract: the build system must scan module dependencies (CMake 3.28+, MSBuild or an equivalent) and every importer is compiled with a compatible compiler and standard.
pitfalls: The whole build must agree: a module and its importers need compatible compilers, flags and module scanning, which is where partial adoption usually stalls.
Macros do not cross module boundaries, so a configuration macro exported by an interface header is silently unavailable to importers.
Cyclic module imports are impossible - a feature that forces the dependency direction to be decided up front instead of being repaired later by an include.
